newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: ANZ sees continued pressure on NZ retail sector.
newsitem.headline: ANZ sees continued pressure on NZ retail sector.

text.p: ANZ Bank said in a report prepared for the New Zealand Retail Merchants Association on Thursday that there was no indication the retail outlook had improved since the sluggish official March quarter data.
"Many retailers had expected a recovery in sales after the disappointing Christmas last year," said ANZ chief economist Paul Stewart, adding "for most stores that is not occurring."

"Those selling large ticket items such as appliances, furniture or motor vehicles have been particularly affected by the weaker sales environment. And there are no indications things have really improved since the March quarter..", he said.

The report said that prices in a number of store types have been falling in recent quarters and a combination of weak demand, high levels of competition to gains sales in a weak spending environment, and the impact of the high NZ dollar on import prices were seen as the factors behind this trend.

"Whereas in recent years higher sales growth has probably enabled some retailers and suppliers to increase margins as the New Zealand dollar rose against most currencies, we are definitely seeing pressure on margins at the current time," Stewart added.
The weaker retail climate is part of an number of signs suggesting the economy is still subdued.
Looking ahead, ANZ's Stewart said, "We expect consumer spending to remain quite weak over the next two to three quarters and advise retailers to proceed cautiously through this period.
"In particular, further falls in sales, particularly of those store types catering for big ticket purchases such as motor vehicles and appliances, cannot be ruled out over coming months," he added.

ANZ does expect the beginnings of a recovery by early 1998, stimulated by recent interest rate falls, a pick-up in world growth and higher levels of government spending which is gradually expected to flow through into renewed retail growth.
